newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries higher at midday on short-covering.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries higher at midday on short-covering.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were higher at midday on Monday as dealers covered short positions, participants said.

"You had a lot of shorts going home in New York on Friday and when they came in on Monday to find the market up, they quickly had to cover," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc.
The market got its initial strength from momentum established overnight related to the dollar's strength, analysts said.

"The dollar reached a 50-month high against the yen and did better against the D-mark," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds. "That's exactly what's going on."
In early afternoon trade, the benchmark 30-year bond was up 15/32 to 94-11, yielding 7.08 percent.
A good swap bid in three-year maturities related to some deals also helped the market, Dimick said.
"There's short-covering and dollar strength is also an element," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
A lack of selling on the upticks was also supportive, participants said.
But analysts were dubious about the ability of the market to advance further.

"This uptrade is coming on very thin volume so I would not assign much significance to it," said Dimick. "It's being driven by the swap-related deals and by the dollar, not by any inherent sense of value in the Treasury market."
"There's nothing fundamental driving it higher," said Moran, who said the market could have a fairly quiet week until Friday.

The government will report producer price and retail sales data on Friday. According to a Reuters poll, the March Producer Price Index (PPI) is forecast at unchanged after falling 0.4 percent in February. Retail sales are forecast to be up 0.6 percent after a 0.8-percent February gain.
"The retail sales data will be important because it's the consumer who seems to be powering the economy and this will give some inkling of their behavior," said Moran.
The Treasury will sell $13.0 billion in three- and six-month bills at its weekly bill auction at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT, a routine event expected to proceed smoothly.
In when-issued trade shortly before the auction, three-month bill rates were 5.14 percent and six-month bill rates were 5.30 percent.

Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.40 percent. In other key issues, the five-year note traded up 4/32 to 99-18/32 to yield 6.73 percent, and the 10-year was up 6/32 to 95-18/32 to yield 6.88 percent.
